label.ta: Exercise 8.1 · Q5 (English only; Tamil review pending)

title.en: Variance and standard deviation of nine wages

q.en: 5. Find the variance and standard deviation of the wages of 9 workers given below: ₹310, ₹290, ₹320, ₹280, ₹300, ₹290, ₹320, ₹310, ₹280.

steps.en: Write the nine wages as the complete data set; n is 9, not 10.
Add the wages and divide by the number of workers to find the mean.
Square the deviations, add them, and divide by the number of observations.
Calculate the population variance, in squared rupees.
Take the positive square root for standard deviation; check with Σx² = 812000.

label.ta: Exercise 8.1 · Q6 (English only; Tamil review pending)

q.en: 6. A wall clock strikes the bell once at 1 o’ clock, 2 times at 2 o’ clock, 3 times at 3 o’ clock and so on. How many times will it strike in a particular day. Find the standard deviation of the number of strikes the bell make a day.

steps.en: A 12-hour clock gives 1 through 12 strikes in sequence, and repeats the same pattern in the second half of a 24-hour day.
The sum of the first 12 natural numbers is 12×13/2 = 78. Double for the entire day.
Compute the mean number of strikes per hour.
The sum of squares of 1 through 12 is 12×13×25/6 = 650; double it.
Use population variance = mean square minus square of the mean.
Take the square root and give the daily strike total separately.
steps.eq: σ = √(143/12) ≈ 3.45 strikes per hour; total daily strikes = 156

records.answer: Total strikes in 24 hours = 156; standard deviation of hourly strike counts = √(143/12) ≈ 3.45.

label.ta: Exercise 8.1 · Q7 (English only; Tamil review pending)

title.en: Standard deviation of the first 21 natural numbers

q.en: 7. Find the standard deviation of first 21 natural numbers.

steps.en: The observations are the natural numbers 1 through 21, so there are 21 values.
Calculate the mean of equally spaced consecutive integers.
Use the formula for the sum of squares of the first n natural numbers.
Use the population variance formula.
Take the square root only after computing the exact variance.
Cross-check with the formula for a uniform sequence 1 to n.

label.ta: Exercise 8.1 · Q8 (English only; Tamil review pending)

title.en: Why subtracting a constant leaves spread unchanged

q.en: 8. If the standard deviation of a data is 4.5 and if each value of the data is decreased by 5, then find the new standard deviation.

steps.en: Let the old observations be x and their old mean be x̄. Every new observation is smaller by 5.
When 5 is subtracted from each value, the mean also decreases by 5.
Compare a new deviation from the new mean with the old deviation.
Because every deviation is unchanged, the mean squared deviation (variance) is unchanged.
Hence the standard deviation remains the original value.

label.ta: Exercise 8.1 · Q9 (English only; Tamil review pending)

q.en: 9. If the standard deviation of a data is 3.6 and each value of the data is divided by 3, then find the new variance and new standard deviation.

steps.en: Dividing each observation by 3 scales every deviation from the mean by the same factor.
Standard deviation scales by the absolute value of the multiplier.
Variance is the square of the standard deviation.
Check using the variance scaling rule directly.

label.ta: Exercise 8.1 · Q10 (English only; Tamil review pending)

title.en: Weighted standard deviation of rainfall data

q.en: 10. The rainfall recorded in various places of five districts in a week are given below. Find its standard deviation. Rainfall (in mm): 45, 50, 55, 60, 65, 70; Number of places: 5, 13, 4, 9, 5, 4.

steps.en: Each rainfall value x occurs at a number of places f, so this is a frequency distribution.
Add all frequencies to find the number of places.
Multiply rainfall by frequency and add to obtain the weighted total.
Calculate the mean weekly rainfall.
Compute the frequency-weighted sum of squared rainfall values.
Use the population frequency-variance formula.
Take the square root, retaining units and rounding only in the final answer.
